steps.t: Three digits Press + and − to build a number. Each digit is worth what its column says. 0 Build a number with the buttons. Look at what each digit is worth. A digit on its own does not tell you how much it is worth. Where it stands does. Press the buttons to build a number. Watch the blocks. A hundred block is a whole square, a ten is a single rod, a one is a little cube. The three in three hundred and forty eight is worth three hundred, because it is standing in the hundreds column. Children read the digits as separate small numbers, three, four, eight. They are not. They are three hundred, and forty, and eight. So build a number, then read what each digit is worth out loud.

Read it and write it Read the number, then tap the words that say it. — Read the number. Tap the words that say it. Numbers are said in the order they are written, hundreds first. Four hundred and seventy two. Four hundred, then seventy, then two. The word and goes in once, after the hundreds, and nowhere else. The teens are the trap. Fourteen is one ten and four ones, but you say the four first. Forty is four tens. Listen for the difference. Read the number, then tap the words that match.

Break it apart Tap the parts that add up to the number. — Tap the three parts that add up to this number. Taking a number apart into its hundreds, its tens and its ones is called decomposing it. Three hundred and forty eight comes apart into three hundred, and forty, and eight. Add those three back together and you have the number again. Nothing is lost and nothing is added. Watch the zero. Three hundred and seven has no tens, so its parts are three hundred and seven, and the zero is holding the tens column open. Tap the three parts that make the number.

Another way to break it Move a hundred across into the tens. The total must not change. ◀ Put one back Move one across ▶ Move one hundred into the tens. The number stays the same. There is more than one way to cut a number up, and every way is still the same number. Three hundred and forty eight is three hundred, forty and eight. It is also two hundred, one hundred and forty, and eight. One hundred moved out of the hundreds and joined the tens as ten tens. That is called regrouping. This looks like a trick until you need it. It is exactly what you do when you take away and the top digit is too small. Move a hundred across and check the total has not changed.

Ten times bigger Press × 10 and watch the digits move one place to the left. × 10 Another number Press times ten and watch every digit move one column left. Multiplying by ten does not add a zero. It moves every digit one column to the left. Thirty five times ten. The three was three tens and becomes three hundreds. The five was five ones and becomes five tens. Nothing is left in the ones, so a zero holds that column open. Three hundred and fifty. Add a zero works here and stops working the moment there is a decimal point. Learn the move, not the trick. Press times ten and watch the digits slide.

steps.h: Count in ones, tens and hundreds
steps.t: Count in ones, tens and hundreds Pick a step, then tap the number that comes next. Pick a start and a step. Then tap the number that comes next. Counting in steps means adding the same amount again and again, from wherever you happen to be. Pick a start and a step. Counting on in tens from two hundred and thirty six gives two hundred and forty six, two hundred and fifty six, two hundred and sixty six. Only the tens digit is moving. Then it crosses a hundred and the hundreds digit moves too. Two hundred and ninety six, then three hundred and six. That is the step everyone gets wrong, so go slowly there. Choose a start, choose a step, and fill in what comes next.

steps.g: comparison odd and even place value statistics subtraction
steps.t: Odd or even Look at the last digit only. Odd or even? — Look at the last digit only. Is it odd or even? A number is even if it can be shared into two equal whole groups, and odd if one is always left over. You do not have to test the whole number. Only the ones digit decides. If it ends in nought, two, four, six or eight it is even, however many hundreds are in front of it. Children look at the first digit because that is the biggest one. It tells you nothing here. Cover the number and leave only the last digit showing. Sort each number into odd or even.

Which is bigger? Tap the sign that belongs between the two numbers. Compare the hundreds first. Tap the sign that goes between them. To compare two numbers, start at the biggest column, not at the end. Look at the hundreds first. If they are different you already have your answer and nothing else matters. If they are the same, move along to the tens, then to the ones. The greater than sign always opens towards the bigger number, like a mouth. The point goes to the smaller one. Tap the sign that belongs between them.

Put them in order Tap them from smallest to biggest . Tap the numbers in order, smallest first. Putting numbers in order is the same comparing, done again and again. Find the smallest of them all and take it first. Then find the smallest of what is left. Keep going until there is nothing left to take. Do not sort by how long a number looks, or by its first digit alone. Ninety nine is shorter than one hundred and one, and smaller. But eighty is shorter than seventy nine, and bigger. Tap them from smallest to biggest.

Round it to 10 or 100 Which neighbour is nearer? Tap the answer. Which neighbour is nearer? Look at the line, then tap. Rounding means picking whichever neighbour is nearer. Find the two tens the number sits between, or the two hundreds. Mark the halfway point. If the number is past halfway it goes up, and if it has not got there yet it goes down. Exactly halfway is nobody nearer, so there is no right answer to find. There is only a rule everyone agreed to follow, and the rule is up. Look at the line, then tap the answer.

Roughly how many? Do not count them all. Pick the closest . Do not count them all. Pick the closest estimate. An estimate is a sensible guess made on purpose, not a wild one. Do not try to count them all. Look at one small group, decide roughly how many are in it, then see how many groups like that would fill the box. An estimate is not a wrong answer. Close is the whole point. If you are within about a hundred here, you estimated well. Have a look, pick the closest, then count a group to check.

Show what you know Tap the answer. Time to show what you know. Tap the answer. Nothing new here. Every question uses something you have already done in this lesson. If it asks what a digit is worth, look at its column. If it asks you to round, find the two neighbours first. If it is a sum, work from the right. Take your time. Read it, think, then tap.

How do you know? Which reason really explains it? Only one of these three reasons really explains it. Which one? Getting the right answer is only half of it. Knowing why it is right is the other half. Here is something that is true. Underneath are three reasons somebody gave for it. Only one of them actually explains it. Watch for a reason that is true and still explains nothing. Both numbers are small can be perfectly true and tell you nothing about why the answer is what it is. Read all three, then pick the one that really does the work.

Make 100, and make 1000 How many more do you need? Tap it. How many more to make the round number? Tap it. A complement is the amount you still need to reach a round number. Sixty two and how many make a hundred? Count on to the next ten first. Sixty two to seventy is eight. Seventy to a hundred is thirty. Eight and thirty is thirty eight. The usual mistake is to make the tens add to ten and forget the ones. Sixty and forty is a hundred, so thirty eight, not forty, once there are ones in the way. Fill the bar to the round number.

Add in any order Tap the two that make a round number first. Find the two that make a round number. Tap them first. Adding can be done in any order you like, and you may join any two of them first. That is not just a fact. It is permission to make the sum easier. In seventeen add nine add three, join the seventeen and the three to make twenty, then add the nine. Twenty nine. Taking away is not like this. Ten take away three is not three take away ten. The freedom belongs to adding only. Find the easy pair, tap those two first.

Adding with regrouping Tap the digit that goes under the line in this column. Work one column at a time, starting at the right. Tap the digit that goes under the line. Add one column at a time, starting from the right. The ones first. If they make ten or more, the extra ten cannot stay in the ones column, so it moves one place left and waits at the top of the tens. That waiting digit is called a carry. The carry is a real number and it has to be added in. Forget it and your answer is out by exactly one ten, which looks so nearly right that nobody notices. Work the ones, then the tens, then the hundreds.

Taking away with regrouping Tap the digit that goes under the line in this column. If the top digit is too small, fetch a ten. Tap the digit that goes under the line. Taking away works down the same columns, from the right. When the digit on top is too small, fetch one from the column to its left. It arrives as ten. Three becomes thirteen, and the column you took it from is one smaller. You may never turn the digits round. Three take away five is not five take away three. That swap is the commonest wrong answer in the whole of subtraction. Exchange when you need to, then take away.

Money and the dot Read the amount. Tap what it is worth. — The dot splits whole shillings from cents. Tap what this amount is worth. The dot in an amount of money separates the whole units from the parts of one. In four point six five, the four is whole shillings and the sixty five is cents. There are always two figures after the dot, because there are a hundred cents in a shilling. Four point five is four shillings and fifty cents, not four and five. The five is sitting in the tens of cents column, so it means fifty. It is place value again, just after a dot. Read the amount, then tap what it is worth.

Giving change Count on from the price. Tap the change. Count on from the price up to what you paid. Tap the change. Change is the difference between what you handed over and what it cost. You can take away, or you can count on, and counting on is usually kinder. From three shillings sixty, count up to four shillings, that is forty cents. Then four to five is one shilling. So one shilling and forty cents. A hundred cents make a shilling, not ten. Counting change in tens is what makes the answer come out wrong. Count on from the price to the note, and tap the change.

Estimate first About how much is it? Before you add or take away, round each number and work out roughly what the answer should be. An estimate is a rough answer you work out first, from easy numbers. 298 add 413. 298 is about 300 and 413 is about 400, so the answer is about 700. The exact answer, 711, is close to 700, so it is probably right. An estimate is not the exact answer, and it is not a guess either. It comes from rounding each number to the nearest hundred. Round each number to the nearest hundred, then add or take away the hundreds.

Shopping with shillings and cents How much altogether? Add the shillings, then add the cents. There are 100 cents in one shilling. To add two prices, add the shillings and then add the cents. sh 12.50 and sh 25.25. The shillings make 12 add 25, which is 37. The cents make 50 add 25, which is 75. Together that is sh 37.75. Keep shillings with shillings and cents with cents. The two figures after the dot are always cents. Add the numbers before the dot, then the numbers after it.

Show what you know Tap the answer. Time to show what you know. Tap the answer. Nothing new here. Every question uses something you have already done in this lesson. If it asks what a digit is worth, look at its column. If it asks you to round, find the two neighbours first. If it is a sum, work from the right. Take your time. Read it, think, then tap.

How do you know? Which reason really explains it? Only one of these three reasons really explains it. Which one? Getting the right answer is only half of it. Knowing why it is right is the other half. Here is something that is true. Underneath are three reasons somebody gave for it. Only one of them actually explains it. Watch for a reason that is true and still explains nothing. Both numbers are small can be perfectly true and tell you nothing about why the answer is what it is. Read all three, then pick the one that really does the work.

Rows and columns Change the rows and the columns. Read it as rows × columns . − row + row − column + column Build rows and columns. Read it as rows times columns. Multiplying is counting equal groups, and an array is those groups laid out in neat rows. Four rows with six in each row. You could count all twenty four one at a time, but you do not need to. Four sixes is twenty four. The groups have to be equal. If one row is short it is not a times fact any more, and counting in that table will give you the wrong answer. Build an array with the buttons and read it out loud.

Turn it round Press Turn and watch the total stay the same. Turn it round Another one Turn the array round. The total does not change. Turning an array on its side does not change how many are in it. Four rows of six is twenty four. Turn it and it is six rows of four, still twenty four. The same dots, looked at another way. So every times fact you learn is really two. This is worth real money to you. Eight nines is hard. Nine eights is the same answer, and if you happen to know that one, you already knew the hard one. Press turn, and watch the total stay put.

The tables you need Tap the answer. — Tap the answer. Ten in a row and you have earned it. These are the tables you are expected to know by heart this year. One, two, three, four, five, six, eight, nine and ten. Knowing them by heart means the answer arrives without working it out. You get there by meeting each fact many times, not by staring at the list. If one will not come, do not just guess. Go to one you do know and step to it. Six sevens. Five sevens is thirty five, and one more seven is forty two. Answer as many as you can.

One array, four facts Tap all four sentences that are true for this array. One array makes four number sentences. Tap the ones that are true. Multiplying and dividing are the same fact, read in different directions. Four sixes are twenty four. So six fours are twenty four. So twenty four shared between four is six, and twenty four shared between six is four. One array, four sentences. This is what to do when a division will not come. Do not hunt for a dividing fact. Ask yourself what you multiply by to get there. Find all four sentences hiding in one array.

Split it to multiply Tap the total. — Split the number into tens and ones, multiply both, then add. A number too big to multiply in one go can be split, multiplied in parts, and added back together. Twenty four times three. Split the twenty four into twenty and four. Twenty threes are sixty. Four threes are twelve. Sixty and twelve is seventy two. Both parts must be multiplied. Multiplying the tens and then forgetting the ones is the mistake that lands you exactly the ones part short. Split it, do both parts, then add.

Estimate, then multiply About how much? Then tap the exact answer. — Round it first to see roughly what to expect. Then tap the real answer. Estimating first tells you what sort of answer to expect, so a silly one cannot slip past. Thirty eight times four. Thirty eight is nearly forty. Forty fours are one hundred and sixty. So the real answer will be a bit under that. An estimate is not the answer and it is not meant to be. It is the fence you check the answer against. Estimate first, then pick the real answer.

Sharing, and what is left How many does each group get? — Share them out equally. How many does each group get, and what is left over? Dividing is sharing into equal groups, and sometimes it does not come out exactly. Deal them out one to each group, round and round, until you cannot give one to everybody. What is left over is the remainder. Here is the check that costs nothing. The remainder must be smaller than the number of groups. If it is not, you stopped a round too early and everybody can still have one more. Share them out, then say how many are left over.

Multiples of 2, 5 and 10 Tap every multiple. Tap every multiple. Look at the last digit. A multiple is a number you land on when you count in steps from zero. You do not have to count all the way there. Multiples of ten end in nought. Multiples of five end in nought or five. Multiples of two end in nought, two, four, six or eight. The last digit tells you. Every multiple of ten is also a multiple of five and of two. So a number can belong to more than one of these, and often does. Tap every multiple you can find.

What is the rule? What is the rule of this sequence? Find the rule first, then the next number. A linear sequence goes up or down by the same amount every time, and that amount is its rule. Find the rule before you find the next number. Take any term away from the one after it. Do it twice to be sure the gap really is the same. Checking one gap is not enough. Two, four, eight looks like adding two until you reach the eight, and then it is not. Say the rule, then say what comes next.

Patterns that grow How many squares in the next picture? Count the squares in each picture. How many in the next one? A pattern can be made of shapes instead of numbers, and it still has a rule. Count the squares in each picture. Write those counts in a row. Now it is a number sequence like any other, and you can find its rule. Look at what is added each time, not at how the shape looks. Two patterns can look completely different and grow by exactly the same amount. Count them, find the rule, then say how many come next.

The mystery box What number is hiding in the box? What number is hiding in the box? When a number is not known yet, we put something in its place to hold the spot. A box, a shape, later a letter. Box add seven is twenty three. The box is not a mystery for ever. Take the seven back off the twenty three and the box has to be sixteen. Look at where the box is standing. Twenty three take away box is seven asks something different from box take away seven is twenty three, and the two have different answers. Work out what is hiding in the box.

Show what you know Tap the answer. Time to show what you know. Tap the answer. Nothing new here. Every question uses something from this lesson. If it is a times fact, think of the array. If it is a division, ask what you multiply by. If it is a sequence, find the rule first. Read it, think, then tap.

How do you know? Which reason really explains it? Only one of these three reasons really explains it. Which one? Getting the right answer is only half of it. Knowing why it is right is the other half. Here is something that is true. Underneath are three reasons somebody gave for it. Only one of them actually explains it. Watch for a reason that is true and still explains nothing. Both numbers are small can be perfectly true and tell you nothing about why the answer is what it is. Read all three, then pick the one that really does the work.

Equal parts, or not Tap the shape cut into equal parts. Which shape is cut into equal parts? Equal means all the same size. A fraction is one or more of several equal parts. Equal is the word that does the work. Look at each shape. If the pieces are all the same size, the shape is cut into fractions. If one piece is bigger than another, it is cut into parts, but they are not fractions. Cut in half means two pieces the same. Two pieces where one is bigger is not a half, however neat the line looks. Tap the shape that really is cut into equal parts.

All the parts make one Tap the pieces. The bottom number stays still; only the top one counts. Colour the pieces. All of them together make one whole. All the parts, taken together, make exactly one whole. Colour in the pieces one at a time and watch the fraction climb. Four quarters is not almost one. It is one. The bottom number never changes as you colour. It says how many pieces the whole was cut into, and that was decided before you started. Only the top number counts what you have taken. Fill it right up and see the whole come back.

Same fraction, different shape Tap every picture showing this fraction. Different shapes, same fraction. Tap all the ones that match. What makes a half a half is the size of the part next to the whole, not the shape it happens to be. A square cut down the middle, a square cut corner to corner, a circle cut across. All different shapes. Every one of them is a half. Turning a shape round does not change its fraction either. A quarter standing on its point is still a quarter. Find every picture showing the fraction asked for.

A fraction of a group How many is this? Share the group into equal piles, then take the piles the fraction asks for. A fraction can describe equal parts of a group of things, not only of one shape. Twelve counters, and you want a quarter of them. Share the whole group into four equal piles, then take one pile. Three. The bottom number tells you how many piles to make, not how many to take. Making four piles and then taking four is the mistake to watch for. Share them into piles, then take the ones you need.

The line means divide Which division does this fraction mean? The fraction line means divide. Match the fraction to its division. The line in a fraction is a dividing line, and it means exactly that. One half is one shared between two. One quarter is one shared between four. Three quarters is three shared between four. So finding a half of twenty is the same as twenty divided by two. This is why halving and dividing by two feel like the same thing. They are the same thing, written two different ways. Match each fraction to the division it means.

A fraction of a number What is this? Divide by the bottom number, then multiply by the top one. A fraction can act on a number. It takes a whole amount and hands back a part of it. A third of eighteen. Divide by the bottom number to find one part. Eighteen divided by three is six. Then multiply by the top number. One third, so one six. Six. Divide first, multiply second. For three quarters of twenty, twenty divided by four is five, and three fives are fifteen. Doing it the other way round is where the answer goes wrong. Divide by the bottom, multiply by the top.

The same, in different pieces Which fraction is worth the same? These two bars are shaded the same amount. Which fraction matches? Two fractions that look completely different can be worth exactly the same. One half and two quarters. Different numbers, same amount of the bar coloured in. Cutting each piece in two doubles how many pieces there are and doubles how many you take, so nothing has actually moved. Bigger numbers do not make a bigger fraction. Five tenths is not more than one half. It is one half. Line the bars up and find the pair that match.

Adding and taking away pieces What is the answer? Count the pieces. The bottom number never changes. When the pieces are all the same size you can simply count them. Two fifths and one fifth. Two pieces and one more piece is three pieces, and they are all fifths. Three fifths. The bottom number does not get added. Two fifths and one fifth is three fifths, never three tenths. You counted pieces. You did not change their size. Count the pieces, and keep the bottom number where it is.

Which is bigger? Tap the sign that goes between them. Look at the bars. Which fraction is bigger? Comparing fractions works differently depending on which number is the same. If the bottom numbers match, the pieces are the same size, so more pieces means more. Three fifths beats two fifths. But if the top numbers are both one, it turns round. One quarter is bigger than one tenth, because sharing between fewer people gives everybody more. The bigger bottom number makes the smaller piece. Look at the bars, then tap the sign.

Show what you know Tap the answer. Time to show what you know. Tap the answer. Nothing new here. Every question uses something from this lesson. If it asks for a fraction of a number, divide by the bottom then multiply by the top. If it asks which is bigger, look at which number is the same first. Read it, think, then tap.

How do you know? Which reason really explains it? Only one of these three reasons really explains it. Which one? Getting the right answer is only half of it. Knowing why it is right is the other half. Here is something that is true. Underneath are three reasons somebody gave for it. Only one of them actually explains it. Watch for a reason that is true and still explains nothing. Both numbers are small can be perfectly true and tell you nothing about why the answer is what it is. Read all three, then pick the one that really does the work.

Naming flat shapes Count the sides. What is this shape called? Count the straight sides, then tap the name of the shape. A flat shape is named by what it has, not by what it looks like to you. Count the straight sides. Three is a triangle. Four is a quadrilateral. Five is a pentagon, six a hexagon, eight an octagon. The corners always come to the same number as the sides. Turning a shape does not rename it. A square standing on its corner is still a square, even when everybody in the room wants to call it a diamond. Count the sides, then tap the name.

Regular or irregular Which of these is regular ? Regular means every side the same length. Which one is regular? A regular polygon has all its sides the same length and all its corners the same. Both of these have five sides, so both are pentagons. Only one of them is regular. The other is stretched, and a stretched pentagon is still a pentagon. Irregular does not mean it is not a proper shape. It only means the sides are not all the same. Most shapes in the real world are irregular. Which one has all its sides the same?

Lines of symmetry Is the dashed line a line of symmetry? Would the shape fold exactly onto itself along the dashed line? A line of symmetry is a fold line where the two halves land exactly on top of each other. Try the fold in your head. Down the middle, and across the middle. If every part matches, that line is a line of symmetry. Cutting a shape into two equal pieces is not enough. The two pieces must be mirror images, not just the same size. Does the dashed line fold this shape onto itself?

Mirror it Tap the squares where the reflection goes. Tap the squares where the reflection belongs, the same distance the other side. A reflection flips a shape over a mirror line. Every point ends up the same distance from the line, on the other side. Work one square at a time. If a square is two along from the mirror, its reflection is two along on the other side. Not three, not one. A reflection is not a slide. Sliding keeps the shape facing the same way. Reflecting turns it round, so what was nearest the mirror is still nearest the mirror. Tap the squares where the reflection goes.

Solid shapes Which solid shape is this? Faces, edges and corners. Which solid shape is it? A solid shape is named by its faces, its edges and its corners. A face is a flat surface. An edge is where two faces meet. A corner is where edges meet. A cube has six faces, twelve edges and eight corners. A drawing of a solid is flat, so some faces are hidden round the back. Count what must be there, not only what you can see. Read the clues and name the solid.

All the way round What is the perimeter? Add up every side, all the way round the outside. The perimeter is the whole distance round the outside of a shape. Start at one corner and walk right round, adding each side as you pass it, until you are back where you began. A rectangle has four sides, so four lengths get added, not two. Only two numbers are usually written on a rectangle, because the other two are the same. They still have to be added. Forgetting them halves the answer. Add up every side, all the way round.

Counting the space inside How many squares does it cover? Count the squares covered inside the shape. Area is how much flat space a shape covers inside its edge. On a grid you can simply count the squares inside the shape. Perimeter is the fence. Area is the field. These two do not grow together. Two shapes can cover the same number of squares and have completely different distances round the edge. Count the squares inside.

Draw it yourself Tap two opposite corners to draw the rectangle. Start again Tap one corner, then the opposite corner, to draw the rectangle. Drawing a shape to a given size is how you find out whether you really understand it. Tap one corner, then tap the opposite corner. Count the squares along the top for the width and down the side for the height. A square is a rectangle whose width and height happen to match. Count the squares, not the lines round them. A rectangle four squares wide has five lines down it, and it is the squares you want. Draw it, then read off its perimeter and its area.

Show what you know Tap the answer. Time to show what you know. Tap the answer. Nothing new here. Every question uses something from this lesson. If it is a shape, count the sides. If it is a measurement, check the unit first. If it is a time, count on. Read it, think, then tap.

How do you know? Which reason really explains it? Only one of these three reasons really explains it. Which one? Getting the right answer is only half of it. Knowing why it is right is the other half. Here is something that is true. Underneath are three reasons somebody gave for it. Only one of them actually explains it. Watch for a reason that is true and still explains nothing. Both numbers are small can be perfectly true and tell you nothing about why the answer is what it is. Read all three, then pick the one that really does the work.

Centimetres, metres, kilometres Choose the answer. A hundred centimetres in a metre, a thousand metres in a kilometre. Length is measured in centimetres, metres and kilometres, and they step up in known jumps. A hundred centimetres make one metre. A thousand metres make one kilometre. So going up a unit means dividing, and coming down means multiplying. Pick the unit that gives a sensible number. A pencil is about fifteen centimetres. Nobody measures a pencil in kilometres, and nobody measures a journey in centimetres. Choose the right unit, or change one into another.

Grams and kilograms Choose the answer. A thousand grams make one kilogram. Pick the sensible answer. Mass is how heavy something is, measured in grams and kilograms. A thousand grams make one kilogram. An apple is about a hundred grams. A bag of rice is a kilogram or two. Big does not mean heavy. A huge bag of feathers can weigh less than a small stone, so guess by what a thing is made of, not by its size. Pick the sensible mass.

Millilitres and litres Choose the answer. A thousand millilitres make one litre. Capacity is how much a container holds, measured in millilitres and litres. A thousand millilitres make one litre. A teaspoon is about five millilitres. A big bottle of water is one or two litres. Millilitres are very small, so the numbers get big quickly. Half a litre is five hundred millilitres, not fifty. Pick the sensible amount.

Reading a scale What is the arrow pointing at? Work out what one mark is worth first, then read the arrow. Before you read any scale, work out what one small mark is worth. Find two numbers that are printed on it. Take one away from the other, then count the gaps between them. Share the difference between the gaps and you know what one mark means. Count the gaps, not the marks. Between two printed numbers with five little lines there are six gaps, and it is the gaps that carry the value. Work out one mark, then read the arrow.

steps.h: Bigger or smaller than a right angle
steps.t: Bigger or smaller than a right angle Compare it with a right angle. Compare this angle with a right angle. Smaller, the same, or bigger? A right angle is the square corner, the quarter turn. Every other angle is measured against it. So each angle is smaller than the square corner, the same, or bigger. Two right angles together make a straight line, which is a half turn. How long the arms are drawn makes no difference at all. The angle is the amount of turn between them, not the size of the picture. Compare it with the square corner and choose.

Measure from any mark How long is it? A ruler does not have to start at zero. Count on from where it starts to where it ends. The length of something is the gap from where it starts to where it ends. A pencil starts at the 2 and ends at the 9. Count on from 2 to 9: that is 7 centimetres. Reading only the end gives 9, which is too long, because the pencil did not start at 0. The start matters as much as the end. Find the start and the end, then count on the centimetres between them.

steps.h: Two right angles, one straight line
steps.t: Two right angles, one straight line How many right angles? Every square corner is one right angle. Two of them side by side make a straight line. A right angle is a quarter turn. Two right angles make a straight line, which is a half turn. Start with an arm pointing right. Turn it one right angle and it points up. Turn it another right angle and it points left, and the two arms now make one straight line. A straight line does not look like an angle, but it is one. It is two right angles put side by side. Count the little square corners. Each one is a right angle.

Show what you know Tap the answer. Time to show what you know. Tap the answer. Nothing new here. Every question uses something from this lesson. If it is a shape, count the sides. If it is a measurement, check the unit first. If it is a time, count on. Read it, think, then tap.

How do you know? Which reason really explains it? Only one of these three reasons really explains it. Which one? Getting the right answer is only half of it. Knowing why it is right is the other half. Here is something that is true. Underneath are three reasons somebody gave for it. Only one of them actually explains it. Watch for a reason that is true and still explains nothing. Both numbers are small can be perfectly true and tell you nothing about why the answer is what it is. Read all three, then pick the one that really does the work.

Telling the time What time is it? The short hand gives the hour, the long hand gives the minutes. The two hands do different jobs, and the short one matters most. The short hand gives the hour, and it creeps along, so read the number it has just passed. The long hand gives the minutes. Each number it points at is five minutes. At twenty five to four the short hand is nearly at four, and the time is still three something. Read the hour the hand has passed, not the one it is heading for. Read the clock, then tap the digital time.

How long did it take? How long is that? — to — Count on from the start time to the end time. A time is a point in the day. A time interval is how long something lasts. They are two different things. To find how long, count on from the start to the end. Go up to the next whole hour first, then count the whole hours, then the last few minutes. You cannot take one time away from the other like ordinary numbers, because an hour is sixty minutes and not a hundred. Counting on never goes wrong that way. Count on from the start time to the end time.

Reading a timetable Read the timetable. Find the row, then look along it to the right column. A timetable is a list of times, read down a column or across a row. Find the row for the place you want, then look along it to the bus you are catching. Put a finger on the row so your eye does not slide onto the wrong line. Every column is one whole journey, and the times in it always go forwards. If your answer goes backwards in time, you have read across two different journeys. Read the timetable and answer the question.

North, south, east, west Which way? North is up, south is down, east is right, west is left. North, south, east and west are the four cardinal points, and they never move. North is up the map, south is down, east is to the right and west is to the left. Never eat soggy weetabix, going round clockwise from the top. Left and right depend on which way you are facing. North does not. That is exactly why directions are given this way. Move the counter the way you are told.

Which unit of time? About how long does it take? Choose the unit that fits: seconds for very short things, then minutes, hours, days, weeks, months and years. Pick the unit of time that gives a sensible number for the thing you are timing. Amina walks to school in about 15 minutes. 15 seconds is far too quick, and 15 hours is far too long, so minutes is the unit that fits. Every answer has the same number, so the number does not help. Picture how long the thing really takes, then choose the unit. Picture the thing happening, then choose seconds, minutes, hours, days, weeks, months or years.

Which bus do you catch? Which bus? A timetable is for planning. Find the bus that gets you there in time, or the first one you can still catch. A timetable helps you plan a journey, not just read a time. Hodan must be at the Library by 10:00. Bus 3 gets there at 10:10, too late. Bus 2 gets there at 9:45, so Bus 2 is the bus to catch. Read down the column for one bus and along the row for one stop. Mixing up a row and a column gives a time from the wrong bus. Find the row you need first, then look along it bus by bus.

Find your way Where are you? Use north, south, east and west to follow a route on the map, and to give one. On a map, north is up, south is down, east is right and west is left. Start at the Home. Go 2 squares east, then 2 squares north, and you reach the School. To give that route to somebody else, you say exactly the same thing. North and south are easy to swap. North is always towards the top of the map, whichever way you are facing. Put your finger on the start, and move it one square at a time as you read.

A question worth asking Which one do you need to collect data to answer? Which question needs data? One where the answers would be different for different people. Some questions need data to answer them, and some do not. How many legs has a spider? You just know that. One answer, the same for everybody, and no counting needed. How do the children in this class travel to school? Nobody knows until somebody asks them all. That is a statistical question. The test is whether the answers would vary. If everybody would say the same thing, there is nothing to collect. Which of these needs you to go and ask people?

Tally marks and totals How many is this tally? Count the bundles in fives, then add the single marks on the end. A tally chart is for counting things as they arrive, when you cannot go back and start again. One mark for each one. When you get to the fifth, lay it across the other four like a gate. Now every bundle is worth five and you can count the bundles in fives. The fifth mark is not an extra one. It is the fifth, lying across. Counting it as a sixth is what makes a tally come out one too many. Count the bundles in fives, then add on the ones left over.

Reading a pictogram How many is that? Read the key first. One picture may stand for more than one. In a pictogram one picture can stand for more than one thing, and the key tells you how many. Read the key first, every single time. If one picture means two, then five pictures mean ten, not five. Half a picture means half of whatever the key says. If a picture is worth ten, half a picture is five. Counting the pictures instead of reading the key is the mistake this chart is designed to catch. Read the key, then work out the row.

Reading a bar chart Read the chart. Look along the bottom for what, and up the side for how many. A bar chart shows how many by how tall. Look along the bottom for what each bar is, and up the side for how many. Run your finger from the top of a bar across to the numbers to read it off. Check what the side scale counts in. If it goes up in twos, a bar reaching the third line is six, not three. Read the chart and answer the question.

A Venn diagram Where does it go? Ask both questions about the number, then tap where it belongs. A Venn diagram sorts things into hoops, and the hoops overlap. Anything in the middle belongs to both hoops at once. Anything outside both hoops still belongs on the picture, it just has neither. Ask both questions about every single item. Is it this? Is it that? Yes and yes goes in the middle. No and no goes outside. Put the number in the right part of the picture.

A Carroll diagram Which box does it belong in? One question across the top, one down the side. Which box? A Carroll diagram sorts by yes and no instead of by hoops. One question runs across the top and the other down the side. Every box is one pair of answers, and every thing belongs in exactly one box. It holds the same information as a Venn diagram. The bottom right box, not this and not that, is the same as being outside both hoops. Answer both questions, then choose the box.

What does it tell you? Answer the question about the chart. What does the data actually show? Read it carefully. Collecting the data is only half of it. The point is what it tells you. Look for the biggest and the smallest. Look for two that are the same. Look at the difference between them, and at the total altogether. Say only what the data actually shows. A chart of this class tells you about this class. It does not tell you about the school, and it does not tell you why. Read the chart, then answer the question about it.

Which one should you use? Which way of showing the data suits this job? Read the situation. Which way of showing the data suits it best? Every way of showing data is good at one thing and poor at another. Choosing well is part of the mathematics. A tally is for counting things as they arrive, when you cannot go back. A bar chart is for seeing at a glance which is biggest. A pictogram is a bar chart made of pictures, with a key. A Venn diagram shows what belongs to both. A Carroll diagram gives a box to all four yes and no answers. There is often more than one that would work. What matters is being able to say why the one you picked suits the job. Read the situation, then choose the way of showing it.

Will, might, will not Will it happen? Will it happen, might it, or will it not? Some things will happen, some might, and some will not. The sun will rise tomorrow. It might rain. A cat will not do your homework. Most things in life sit in the middle, in the might. Might is not the same as will not. You might not roll a six on your next go, and sixes still come up all the time. Save will not for things that truly cannot happen. Where on the line does this one belong?

Try it and see Spin the arrow and keep the score. Spin Spin 20 times Spin it many times and keep the score. A few spins prove nothing. A chance experiment is trying something many times and writing down what happened. Spin the arrow again and again and keep the score. The biggest colour comes up most, because there is more room for the arrow to land on it. A few spins prove nothing. The smallest colour can easily win the first three. It is only after many, many spins that the counts start to look like the spinner. Spin it plenty of times and watch what happens.
